title: Caliph al-Mutawakkil and his Court Singer Mahbubah

full_text:
In the palace of Samarra, the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mutawakkil had in his court a singer of sublime talent and poetic sensitivity named Mahbubah. She had been educated in all the refined arts of the golden age, and her compositions on the lute were celebrated for their emotional depth and delicate nuance.

Unlike many flatterers who courted royal favor for gold and estates, Mahbubah’s devotion to the Caliph was founded on sincere gratitude for his patronage of the arts and his generous protection of poets and scholars.

When courtly intrigue and political turbulence suddenly swept over the capital, Caliph Al-Mutawakkil perished, and a new regime seized power in Samarra. The fickle courtiers immediately pledged allegiance to the new rulers, casting aside their mourning garments and celebrating in the banqueting halls.

Mahbubah alone refused to sing songs of hollow praise for the usurpers. She retired to her private chambers, dressed in simple mourning garments, tuned her lute to the ancient elegiac modes, and composed moving verses lamenting the transience of worldly splendor and celebrating the generous spirit of the fallen monarch.

When the new sovereign summoned her to court, commanding her to perform celebratory melodies, Mahbubah stood with quiet dignity, touched the strings of her lute, and sang her elegies of faithful memory with such heartbreaking beauty, sincerity, and sorrow that the entire assembly—including the new ruler—wept openly in their robes.

Moved by her unshakeable fidelity, the new sovereign did not punish her; instead, he bowed before her artistic integrity, granted her complete freedom and a royal pension, and allowed her to retire to Baghdad in peace, where her verses were preserved for centuries as a monument to true loyalty that refuses to compromise with the changing winds of power.
moral: True loyalty and poetic fidelity outlive earthly power, honoring the memory of kindness with enduring art.
